hook.support: Think of a horror trailer. You can *hear* it: a low hum, then silence, then a scream. Nobody told you to feel scared. The **pictures and sound** did.
hook.core: Close your eyes and think of a horror film trailer. You can probably *hear* it: the low hum, the sudden silence, the scream. Now picture a car ad: wide open road, sunset, a song that makes you want to drive. Nobody told you how to feel. The **pictures and sound** did.

why.support: Films, ads and videos use **pictures**, **colour**, **music** and **sound**. They're all chosen on purpose. Learn to read them, and you'll see what a text is really saying.
why.core: Most texts you see each day aren't just words. Films, ads, posters, videos and safety signs all use **images**, **colour**, **music** and **sound effects** to make meaning. Every one of those is chosen on purpose. When you can read them, you understand what a text is really saying, and you can use them when you make your own.
why.extend: Visual and auditory cues carry meaning alongside, and sometimes instead of, words. Camera shots, colour, layout, music and sound effects are deliberate choices. Annotating them, and inferring what they suggest, lets you interpret how a text creates meaning and positions its audience.

articles.title: Reading pictures and sound

body.support:
Videos and posters use **picture clues** and **sound clues**. They're chosen on purpose.

**Picture clues**

- **Close-up**: you feel what the person feels.
- **Wide shot**: you see the whole place.
- **Colour**: red can mean danger. Blue can feel calm.
- **Big and bright**: you notice it first.

**Sound clues**

- **Music**: fast is exciting. Slow is sad.
- **Sound effects**: a siren warns you.
- **Silence**: makes you hold your breath.

**Work it out.** Texts don't always say what they mean. You **infer** it. Grey rain, then bright sun, after a pill? The ad wants you to think the pill helps.

**Annotate.** Draw an arrow to each clue. Write what it makes you feel.
body.core:
When you watch a video or look at a poster, words are only part of the message. The rest comes from **visual cues** (what you see) and **sound cues** (what you hear). They're always chosen on purpose.

**Visual cues**

- **Shots.** A **close-up** gets near a face, so you feel what the person feels. A **wide shot** shows the whole scene, so you see where you are, or how alone someone is. A camera looking *up* at someone makes them seem powerful.
- **Colour.** Red can mean danger, heat or love. Blue can feel calm, or cold. Bright, warm colours feel happy. Grey feels sad or dull.
- **Layout.** On a poster, the biggest, brightest thing in the centre is what you notice first. Designers put the most important message there.
- **Symbols.** A red cross means first aid. A tick means *yes* or *done*. A symbol can say a lot without any words.

**Sound cues**

- **Music** sets the mood. Fast and upbeat feels exciting. Slow, low notes feel sad or scary. A **jingle** is a short, catchy song that helps you remember.
- **Sound effects** add meaning: a siren warns, a heartbeat builds tension.
- **Voice.** A calm voice reassures. A shout grabs attention.
- **Silence.** A sudden silence makes you hold your breath.

**Reading between the lines.** Texts often don't *say* what they want you to think. You **infer** it from the cues. If an ad shows grey rain *before* someone takes a pill and bright sunshine *after*, it's suggesting the pill makes life better, without saying so.

**How to annotate.** Draw arrows to each cue, label it, and write what it makes the audience think or feel.
body.extend:
In multimodal texts, meaning comes from **visual** and **auditory** cues as well as words. These cues are chosen on purpose. Reading them matters as much as reading the words.

**Visual cues**

- **Shot type and angle:** a **close-up** brings us close to someone's feelings. A **wide shot** shows the setting, or how isolated someone is. A low angle makes a person look powerful; a high angle makes them look small.
- **Colour:** red can suggest danger or passion; blue, calm or coldness. These meanings depend on context and culture.
- **Layout:** size, brightness and central placement guide the viewer's eye to what the designer wants seen first.
- **Symbols:** images with agreed meanings, like a red cross or a tick.

**Auditory cues**

- **Music** sets mood and pace. A **jingle** sticks in memory through repetition and rhythm.
- **Sound effects** add realism or tension.
- **Voice** (calm, urgent, warm) shapes how a message is received.
- **Silence** creates emphasis by contrast.

**Inference.** Multimodal texts often suggest rather than state. Putting a grey, rainy *before* next to a bright *after* suggests a product changes lives, without making a claim anyone could test. Working out these hidden meanings is central to critical viewing.

**Annotation** makes your analysis visible. Find each cue, name it precisely, and explain its effect on the audience.

caseStudies.title: The jingle that stuck

body.support:
In the 1980s, lots of Australians got skin cancer. **Cancer Council Victoria** wanted people to protect themselves from the sun.

In **1981**, they made an ad with a cartoon seagull called **Sid**. Sid danced and sang a catchy song: *Slip! Slop! Slap!* Slip on a shirt. Slop on sunscreen. Slap on a hat.

The clues:

- **Sound:** a bouncy, catchy song.
- **Pictures:** a bright, friendly cartoon.
- **Words:** three short, rhyming actions.

People still remember it. In **2023**, it was added to a list of official **Sounds of Australia**.
body.core:
In the early 1980s, Australia had very high rates of skin cancer. The Anti-Cancer Council of Victoria (now **Cancer Council Victoria**) wanted people to protect themselves from the sun. But how do you get a whole country to remember?

In **1981**, they launched an ad with a cartoon character: **Sid the Seagull**. Sid danced on the beach in board shorts and sang a short, catchy **jingle**: *Slip! Slop! Slap!* Slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat.

The jingle was written by **Phillip Adams** and composed by **Peter Best**. They adapted it from a Queensland campaign called *Slip Slop Shove*.

Think about the cues:

- **Sound:** a bouncy, repeated jingle that's easy to remember.
- **Visuals:** a bright, friendly cartoon instead of scary pictures.
- **Words:** three short actions that rhyme and are easy to say.

It was so catchy that many people who were kids in the 1980s can still sing it. In **2023**, the **National Film and Sound Archive** added the jingle to its **Sounds of Australia** list, alongside famous Australian songs.

The message was serious, but the pictures and sound made it fun, friendly and impossible to forget.
body.extend:
In the early 1980s, skin cancer rates in Australia were very high. The Anti-Cancer Council of Victoria (now **Cancer Council Victoria**) needed a health message that would reach the whole population, and stay with them.

In **1981**, it launched a TV ad starring **Sid the Seagull**, a cartoon seagull in board shorts. Sid sang a short **jingle**: *Slip! Slop! Slap!* **Phillip Adams** wrote it and **Peter Best** composed it. They adapted it from a Queensland Cancer Fund campaign, *Slip Slop Shove*.

The ad's cues work together:

- **Sound:** a bouncy, repeated jingle with a strong rhythm that's easy to remember.
- **Visuals:** a bright, friendly cartoon instead of confronting medical images. This keeps the tone positive and suits children.
- **Words:** three one-syllable commands that start with the same sound and are easy to recall.

The jingle became part of Australian culture. In **2023**, the **National Film and Sound Archive** added it to its **Sounds of Australia** list.

The case shows how playful visual and sound choices can carry a serious message, and how sound can make a text memorable for decades.

model.text:
**The video:** A 30-second road safety ad about using your phone while driving.

**0 to 5 s. Picture:** A close-up of a phone lighting up. **Sound:** A cheerful message tone. **Effect:** It feels normal. This could be me.

**5 to 20 s. Picture:** The camera stays on the driver's eyes as they look down. **Sound:** The music fades to nothing. **Effect:** The silence builds tension.

**20 to 30 s. Picture:** A black screen with white text. **Sound:** One message tone, then nothing. **Effect:** We imagine the crash. That is stronger than seeing it.
why: It notes the picture **and** the sound for each part.
It uses the right terms, like close-up and fade.
It explains the effect on the audience each time.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read visual cues (shot type and angle, colour, layout, symbols) and auditory cues (music, sound effects, voice, silence) in films, ads, posters and videos, and to infer implied meanings. They annotate a poster and a real video, and the case study is Cancer Council Victoria's 1981 Slip! Slop! Slap! ad with Sid the Seagull, added to the National Film and Sound Archive's Sounds of Australia in 2023. Extend students compare two texts on the same topic.

Bring real posters, or print some (workplace safety posters work well for VM).

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** visual: shots, colour, layout, symbols; sound: music, effects, voice, silence. A close-up is near a face or object (personal); a wide shot shows the whole scene. To infer is to work out what a text suggests without saying it.

**Poster:** 1 colour (danger, warning); 2 close-up (personal); 3 layout (noticed first); 4 symbol (warning without words); 5 detail (read after the main message); 6 logo (who's behind it).

**Mood (samples):** smiling close-up — happy, warm; something good is happening. Grey rain and an unanswered phone — worried, lonely; something's wrong. Silence then heartbeat — tense; something scary is about to happen. Low angle on a shouting coach — powerful, intimidating; the coach is in charge.

**Case study:** sound: a bouncy, repetitive jingle; visual: a bright cartoon seagull; words: three short rhyming actions. A cartoon keeps it friendly and suits kids and families; scary images might make people switch off. It's catchy, repeated and simple.

realityCheck: **Watching with and without sound** is the most powerful activity. Students are often surprised by how much the music does.
**Choose videos carefully.** Avoid ads for alcohol, gambling and vaping, and check trailers for age ratings.
**Colour meanings aren't universal.** Invite students to share what colours mean in their cultures.
**Some students are visual thinkers.** Sketching and labelling may suit them better than writing paragraphs.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It leads into Make a Podcast in Digital Life.
